why: With one fixed direction, the flow across each edge is a running sum of (products[i] - avg), shifted by a constant that depends on where the flow starts. To make every edge's flow non-negative the shift must cancel the minimum prefix, so the clockwise cost is sum(prefix) - n*min(prefix); counter-clockwise is the mirror, n*max(prefix) - sum(prefix).
hints: Fix the direction as clockwise. How many products cross the edge between container i and i+1? It depends on the surplus accumulated before it.

Let P[i] = sum of (products[j] - avg) for j <= i. The flow over edge i is P[i] + c for some constant c, every flow must be >= 0 because products only move one way, and the cost is the sum of flows. The smallest valid c is -min(P).
One pass computes the prefix values, their sum, min and max: clockwise = sum(P) - n*min(P), counter-clockwise = n*max(P) - sum(P); return the smaller. O(n), 64-bit arithmetic.
pitfalls: Products may not move backwards, so you cannot use the median trick from the two-way circular version; the answer depends on min or max of the prefix sums.
Try both directions; they can give different costs (8 vs 7 in the example).
constraints:
• Not stated in the source screenshots. Reasonable bounds: 1 <= n <= 10^5, 0 <= products[i] <= 10^9, and sum(products) is divisible by n.
  • The answer may exceed the 32-bit integer range.
